summary:
MarsWalk is a route planner and walking guide for astronauts on foot at Mount Sharp’s boxwork region in Gale Crater, where Curiosity is working today.

It has three screens that run offline in the browser. Plan builds a route between science stops on a 2 km map from NASA’s 1 m HiRISE elevation model. Each route weighs several data layers together instead of slope alone: suit slope limits, ground Curiosity has already driven, radio shadow from the habitat, boxwork ridges and a radiation-shelter map calibrated with Curiosity’s RAD measurements. Walk is a wrist display. It counts down to the latest moment to turn back, estimates oxygen, checks before each stop whether there is time to continue, and plans a direct path home when it is shorter. Helmet Camera runs a model trained on NASA’s AI4Mars labels to mark loose sand in rover photos.

This answers the Martian Map challenge by turning NASA orbital and rover data into decisions an astronaut can act on: which way to go, and when to turn back. On Mars there is no GPS and no live link to Earth, so every number is shown as an estimate and its source is documented.
details:
MarsWalk is a website we built to help an astronaut plan a walk and get back home safely, at the Mount Sharp boxwork region in Gale Crater where Curiosity is driving right now. On the planning screen you pick a few science stops on a 2 km map made from NASA’s HiRISE elevation data, and the site draws two routes for you: the shortest one and the one with the lowest estimated risk. For risk we didn’t want to look at slope alone, so we added other layers on top of it: ground Curiosity has already driven on, places where the habitat’s radio can’t reach, boxwork ridges we found in HiRISE images, and a radiation shelter map based on a real RAD measurement Curiosity made at Murray Buttes. You can turn each layer on and off and see how the route changes.

The second screen is meant for a phone on the wrist. During the walk it tells the astronaut how long they have before they must turn back, roughly how much oxygen is left, and at each stop whether there is enough time to go on. If they turn back, it finds a direct way home when that is shorter than retracing the route. The third screen is an experiment: a small model we trained on NASA’s AI4Mars dataset marks loose sand in rover photos, and it runs right in the browser without internet.

We prepared the data with Python, trained the model with PyTorch on Colab, and wrote the website in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript so it works offline. Since there is no GPS on Mars and no live connection to Earth, everything runs on the device. NASA has walking limits for astronauts on the Moon but not yet for Mars, so we used the Artemis numbers and say so openly. We never call a route “safe”. Anything simulated or assumed is labelled on screen, and every data source is written down in the project.
